name: WiFi (WLAN) Profiles
os_min: Windows Vista (Native Wifi / WLAN AutoConfig service and WLAN_profile XML schema)
location: XML files under %ALLUSERSPROFILE%\Microsoft\Wlansvc\Profiles\Interfaces\{interface-GUID}\{profile-GUID}.xml, one file per saved network per wireless adapter; also queryable live via `netsh wlan show profiles` and `netsh wlan show profile name="SSID" key=clear`.
purpose: Stores every wireless network (SSID) a machine has been configured to connect to, including its authentication/encryption settings and, unless cleared, its pre-shared key — providing SSID connection history and potential credential recovery.
key_fields: sharedKey/protected (true = keyMaterial is DPAPI-encrypted hex; false = keyMaterial is stored as cleartext, as seen in some GPO-deployed profiles)
normal_baseline: One profile per network the user has genuinely joined (home, workplace, known public hotspots); sharedKey/protected is normally "true", meaning keyMaterial is DPAPI-encrypted and unreadable outside the machine/user context that saved it.
anomalies: A profile for an SSID the user denies ever connecting to (rogue AP / evil-twin association, or a profile silently added by a script or malware)
sharedKey/protected set to "false" with the passphrase stored in cleartext, outside of an expected GPO-managed wireless deployment
A burst of new profile files created in a short time window, consistent with a Wi-Fi credential-harvesting tool run rather than normal user connection behavior
Execution of `netsh wlan show profile ... key=clear` or a wireless key-recovery tool shortly before data staging/exfiltration
parsing_tools: netsh wlan show profiles / netsh wlan show profile name=X key=clear (built-in)
Direct XML review of the Wlansvc\Profiles\Interfaces path
anti_forensic_notes: keyMaterial is DPAPI-protected by default (protected="true"), tying decryption to the machine/user context that saved it, which is why recovery is normally done through `netsh ... key=clear` (or an equivalent DPAPI unwrap) run in that same context rather than by reading the XML key material directly. Deleting a saved network removes its XML profile file, and with it the SSID history, leaving only whatever MFT/file-deletion metadata the filesystem retains.
